newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen official warns Russia of guerrilla threat.
newsitem.headline: Chechen official warns Russia of guerrilla threat.

text.p: Chechnya's vice-president warned on Monday that guerrillas hired by Russians hoping to wreck peace efforts in the Caucasus region were planning attacks on three Russian cities, Itar-Tass news agency said.

Vakha Arsanov, deputy to separatist president Aslan Maskhadov, told the agency by telephone that Moscow's "party of war" -- shadowy figures opposed to last summer's peace deal -- planned to pay Chechens to carry out the strikes.
He did not say when they might happen. Arsanov and other officials in the Chechen capital, Grozny, could not be contacted immediately.

Guerrilla leader Salman Raduyev, who refuses to recognise Maskhadov's authority, has threatened attacks on Russian cities next month to mark the first anniversary of a Russian rocket strike against separatist leader Dzhokhar Dudayev on April 20.
The top Chechen leadership says Dudayev died. Raduyev, who made his name with a bloody hostage-taking raid in Dagestan in January 1996, insists Dudayev is alive, though gravely ill.

Arsanov, in his interview with Tass, did not refer to Raduyev by name but said "one of the field commanders, whose name is well known" had been offered about $20 million by the "party of war" to take responsibility for the planned attacks.

But, Arsanov added, a powerful member of a Chechen criminal organisation in Moscow would actually carry out the attacks. This person's family had been taken hostage by the unnamed forces planning the strikes. He had been offered $3 million to carry them out.

Maskhadov's successful military action against the Russian army in Grozny last August led to a ceasefire and the withdrawal of Moscow's troops from the mainly Moslem North Caucasus region after 20 months of fighting.
Negotiations are continuing to establish a lasting peace and economic settlement. Maskhadov is pressing for full Chechen sovereignty but Moscow categorically refuses.
Throughout the war, the Chechen separatists regularly accused some senior Russian officials of profiting from the conflict and of trying to prolong it.

Apart from two spectacular cross-border raids, including that led by Raduyev, there were a number of guerrilla attacks in Russia during the war, which were never explained. These included bombs on the Moscow metro and trolleybuses last summer.
